video_title: Market Bloodbath! What The Heck Just Happened? | Michael Lebowitz
gist: Michael Lebowitz (RIA) reads the post-election 4%+ S&P 500 drop as a technical hedge-fund and positioning washout, not an AI-bubble top, since bonds, gold and the dollar showed no flight to safety. He watches the 200-day moving average and widening low-grade credit spreads, says RIA has rotated back into mega-cap growth, and argues 5% Treasuries offer asymmetric risk/reward worth locking in.

themes.theme: Post-election tech selloff read as technical, not fundamental

insights.claim: Michael Lebowitz attributes the post-election day when the S&P 500 fell more than 4% to technical forces (post-event hedge unwinds, position rebalancing, and likely forced margin liquidation at one or more hedge funds) rather than a fundamental change.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Treat the selloff as a positioning event unless follow-through appears.
insights.quote: I think it was much more technical: deployment of positions, margin calls, whatever it is provoked.

insights.claim: Lebowitz says rumors circulated of a hedge fund blowup or forced margin cover, with roughly 10 names mentioned, though he admits he does not know who, if anyone, it was.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Forced-liquidation flows can exaggerate index moves beyond fundamentals.

insights.claim: Lebowitz argues that if the selloff were the start of a real AI-bubble crash, safe havens would have rallied, yet bonds rose only slightly, gold was flat and the dollar was relatively unchanged.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Check cross-asset flight-to-safety confirmation before calling an equity top.

insights.claim: Before the crash day, hyperscalers such as Amazon and Microsoft rallied 5-7% on Wednesday while long-term AI build-out names (chipmakers, Caterpillar-type infrastructure stocks) were already under pressure and out of favor.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: The damage started in AI-infrastructure names, not the hyperscalers.

insights.claim: Lebowitz compares the episode to the Situational Awareness fund blowup about two months earlier, where Citadel bought its securities at a discount, and suggests other hedge funds knowingly shorted the troubled fund's holdings to create an avalanche.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Predatory selling around a distressed fund can drive outsized sector drops.

insights.claim: Lebowitz says that, unusually, the market heat map turned completely red during the day as the selloff broadened from tech, with the equal-weight S&P down around 3% and the Dow down about 3%, versus the usual half-green, half-red rotation days.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: A fully red tape is a breadth warning worth monitoring if it repeats.

insights.claim: Lebowitz cautions against reacting to anticipated events, citing election night 2016 when S&P futures were down 7-8% overnight on Trump's win but the market ended the next day roughly flat and rallied over the following month.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Let post-event flows settle for a few days before reassessing.

insights.claim: Lebowitz says Nasdaq's 15%+ drawdown from its high is significant but not doomsday given its higher volatility, calling it consolidation rather than a confirmed correction while earnings forecasts remain intact.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Scale drawdowns by the asset's beta before labeling a bear market.

insights.claim: Lebowitz and Lance wanted to buy several beaten-down tech stocks after the close, but those names opened 8-10% higher the next morning, so they held off; the intended move was a small trading add, not a fundamental call.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Oversold snapbacks can be fast; dip-buying windows close quickly.

themes.theme: AI data center politics after the blue wave

insights.claim: Lebowitz argues the election changed little for AI because both parties' voters are pushing back on data centers and most permitting decisions happen at county and state level rather than in Congress or the executive branch.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Federal election outcomes are a weak driver of AI capex timelines.

insights.claim: Lebowitz notes Texas Governor Abbott has already frozen data center permit issuance, Texas being the first or second largest state by data center count.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Local permitting pushback is a real, bipartisan capex risk.

insights.claim: Adam Taggart counters that a larger-than-expected Democratic wave in the Senate and governorships could slow AI data center construction, and that even a 20% slower build schedule would have significant market consequences given AI's weight in markets and the economy.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Capex timing, not just capex occurring, matters for AI-heavy indices.

insights.claim: Lebowitz contends data centers will be built regardless because demand far outstrips supply, and if the US slows them they will be built in Mexico, Canada or elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: AI infrastructure demand may relocate rather than disappear.
insights.quote: We will have data centers. They too valuable.

insights.claim: Lebowitz says hyperscalers earn enough money outside AI to sustain their AI spending, even if some AI stocks are in a bubble and many AI companies will fail, so calling a top now is premature.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Distinguish cash-rich hyperscalers from speculative AI names.

themes.theme: Market technicals: 200-day line and hidden bear market

insights.claim: Lebowitz expects the market to trend upward through year-end on rebalancing and redemption flows but is more worried about next year, when the rate rise of the past five months starts to bite.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Constructive into year-end, cautious on 2027.
insights.quote: I am more I'm more worried about next year than the next few months.

insights.claim: The S&P 500 sits at its 200-day moving average, which Lebowitz calls the key line in the sand; another broad, all-red down day that closes below it could signal a regime change and alter RIA's approach.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Watch the 200-day and breadth over the next one to two weeks.

insights.claim: SPY has gone nowhere since early May apart from a four-day rally in August, trading at the same level on November 7 as on May 7.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Passive index holders have earned roughly nothing for six months.

insights.claim: Lebowitz's own work shows 60% of S&P 500 stocks were at some point this year 20% below their yearly peak, meaning most stocks had a bear market while the index masked it.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Sector and stock rotation mattered more than index direction this year.

insights.claim: The S&P 500 is trading about three standard deviations below its Bollinger Band with RSI, MACD and Williams %R deeply oversold, which Lebowitz says implies a technical rebound, though a declining lower band means the market could ride the band lower.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Expect a bounce; its durability at the 200-day is the real test.

insights.claim: Over the prior 20 trading days, large-cap growth fell about 10% while large-cap value rose, the S&P fell about 5%, a basket of healthcare, staples and real estate gained about 9%, and tech fell about 18%.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Extreme sector dispersion created a large rotation opportunity.

insights.claim: RIA's absolute/relative grid runs each ETF price and its ratio to the S&P 500 through about 13 technical models to score overbought/oversold; it currently shows healthcare (XLV) and staples very overbought and tech very oversold, and MGK mega-cap growth swinging from very overbought on October 1 to very oversold while VTV value moved the opposite way.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Extremes in the grid rarely persist and flag mean-reversion trades.

themes.theme: RIA positioning: rotation back into growth

insights.claim: RIA's factor rotation model switched on Monday before the election to buy growth and sell value, moving the sector-model sleeve from 80/20 value/growth to 80/20 growth/value, which Lebowitz admits may have been slightly premature after the crash day.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: A systematic manager is leaning into oversold mega-cap growth.

insights.claim: RIA's 100%-equity factor rotation model is up 26% year to date versus roughly 7.5-8% for the S&P 500, while its 60/40 portfolio is up about 7.1% with considerably less risk.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Active growth/value rotation has paid off in a sideways index year.

insights.claim: In the stock model RIA trimmed winning value stocks back to model weights, added about 1% in Palo Alto Networks, looked to add cybersecurity, added five or six fast-growing companies, and remains centered on large hyperscalers with exposure to GEV and AMD.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Shows which growth names a rotation manager is buying.

themes.theme: Jobs data and the December Fed hike

insights.claim: Lebowitz dismisses the strong jobs report as one month of data that is often revised down, saying he would need three to four months of confirmation from ADP, JOLTS, ISM and regional Fed surveys before calling the labor market improved.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Do not trade on a single payroll beat.
insights.quote: One month does not create a trend .

insights.claim: Lebowitz says the labor market is a stagnant no-hire, no-fire economy where, if layoffs begin, there will be no cushion because nobody is hiring.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Labor-market downside could be abrupt once layoffs start.

insights.claim: Markets price an 80-90% probability that the Fed hikes in December, and Lebowitz expects the hike unless oil drops sharply, unemployment is revised much higher, or the equity selloff deepens.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: A December hike is largely priced; watch the conditions that would cancel it.

insights.claim: Lebowitz expects further Fed hikes to push long-term yields such as the 10-year lower by raising the odds of disinflation and slower growth, describing the long end as encouraging the Fed to make a policy mistake.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Hikes could flatten the curve and support long bonds.

insights.claim: Adam Taggart notes that stronger jobs data and rising real rates are pressuring gold, since precious metals tend to fall when real rates rise.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Hawkish data is a near-term headwind for gold.

insights.claim: Lebowitz is not convinced the yield peak is in but says a double top in yields, a common and reliable technical signal, looks favorable, and the bearish deficit and dollar-reserve narratives are fading.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: The risk/reward on duration is improving even without a confirmed peak.

insights.claim: Lebowitz says the term premium, not breakeven inflation, drove the sharp rise in yields this year.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: The yield rise was a risk-premium story, not an inflation story.

insights.claim: Higher yields are self-correcting: hyperscalers have started issuing equity instead of debt, and with a large wall of corporate debt maturing over the next year or two, more equity issuance would reduce bond supply.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Shrinking bond supply plus economic drag supports lower future yields.

insights.claim: RIA bought newly auctioned five-year Treasuries at about 5% a month earlier and may add more, and Lebowitz notes strong 10- and 30-year auctions and municipal bond offerings selling out before he can fill orders.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Institutional demand at 5%+ yields is strong.

insights.claim: Lebowitz's bond math: a 5-year bond bought at 5% roughly breaks even after one year if yields rise about 1%, earns about 9% if yields fall to 4%, and about 5% if unchanged; a 2-year needs a roughly 2-2.5% yield rise to break even.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Five-year Treasuries offer asymmetric risk/reward at 5%.

insights.claim: Lebowitz argues that if yields rise to 6% the economy likely weakens toward disinflation, setting up bond gains, while a drop toward 2% would mean stocks are falling, letting bondholders sell bonds to buy cheap stocks.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Bonds at 5% hedge both tails of the macro outcome.

insights.claim: Using a football fourth-down analogy, Lebowitz urges retirement investors to kick the field goal: lock in 5%+ bond yields that reliably meet their goals instead of reaching for extra equity return.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Goal-based investors should add duration while 5% is available.
insights.quote: There are times when it's okay to just kick a field goal.

insights.claim: Adam Taggart says this year saw record equity exposure in portfolios, especially among older investors, which he calls unwise, and frames 5% yields as a train that may soon leave the station.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: Over-equitied investors have a window to rebalance into bonds.

insights.claim: BBB corporate spreads stand at about 116bp over Treasuries, up from about 95bp in September, at the ~98.5th percentile of the past three months but near the 50th percentile over five years and the bottom 15th percentile over 20 years; spreads hit about 140-150bp during the tariff episode.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Investment-grade credit is widening but not yet alarming.

insights.claim: CCC spreads have risen significantly, sit at the 88th percentile over 20 years, and are the second highest reading since COVID, though the CCC index is small and illiquid.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Stress is showing up first in the weakest credits.

insights.claim: Contagion down the credit ladder is starting: single-B spreads began widening relative to AAA only in the last week or two after being in the low single digits, while BB widening remains insignificant.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Watch whether widening climbs from CCC to B to BB.

insights.claim: RIA's new eight-factor liquidity indicator (credit spreads, overnight rates, bank reserves, bond yields, the dollar, price trends and volatility) is declining, driven mostly by banking and financial-system factors.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Liquidity is softening, not panicking.

insights.claim: Bank reserves have fallen slightly below $3 trillion, a level the Fed considers comfortable, and the secured SOFR rate has traded 5-10bp above the unsecured fed funds rate, signs of a small liquidity shortage likely intended by the Fed.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Funding markets are tightening at the margin.

insights.claim: Lebowitz says credit spreads keep him up at night more than anything else, and in 2019 similar liquidity stress (repo strain prompting Fed liquidity injections) led RIA to cut equity exposure; significant further widening would prompt RIA to cut equities again.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Spread widening is the trigger for de-risking.
insights.quote: Credit spreads keep us up at night

themes.theme: Municipal bonds: tax edge vs. liquidity and opacity

insights.claim: With Treasuries near 5%, high-quality corporates yield about 5.30% and tax-advantaged municipal bonds offer tax-equivalent yields of about 5.30-5.40%, but both carry credit-spread risk if spreads widen while Treasury yields fall.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Extra yield over Treasuries comes with spread risk.

insights.claim: Municipal bonds are less liquid than corporates, with wider bid/ask spreads, and their disclosures are more opaque than SEC-filed corporate information, so Lebowitz would all else equal prefer corporate bonds.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Muni investors should plan to hold rather than trade.

insights.claim: Investors in high-tax states like Maryland gain by buying in-state munis exempt from both federal and state income tax, while residents of no-income-tax states can shop munis nationally; a muni yielding about 3.5% can equal 5-5.5% on a tax-equivalent basis.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz
insights.so_what: Compare munis on tax-equivalent yield.
